<section id="overview" class="content-section">

## What is Danaher Armbar System?

**The Danaher Armbar System is a BJJGraph study framework for treating the armbar as an entry, control and decision process before attempting a finish.**

Arm Bars: Enter The System provides a detailed course companion for a familiar problem: reaching an armbar position while the defender can still turn, connect their hands or recover posture. Its published contents separate entry and control from later stages and include work from guard, mount and other positions.

BJJGraph organises those topics below into an original study plan. Begin by identifying which stage is failing in your own rounds. Someone who loses the arm during entry needs a different practice task from someone who retains the position but cannot deal with a defensive grip. Use coached demonstrations for the technical details and treat the control position as a useful stopping point for drills.

</section>

<section id="key-principles" class="content-section">

## Core Principles
- Separate reaching the armbar position from securing the arm.
- Check control of the shoulder as well as the wrist.
- Reassess body orientation when the defender turns instead of pulling harder.
- Treat joined hands as a grip-separation problem before attempting extension.
- Compare top and bottom entries by the control they preserve.
- Release immediately on a tap or request to stop.


</section>

<section id="key-components" class="content-section">

## Key Components
**Entry selection** (Locate the start of the control task.)
Choose a guard or mount entry and identify the moment the targeted arm becomes separated from the defender's torso.

**Armbar position retention** (Find the source of an escape before discussing the finish.)
Check whether the defender can withdraw the elbow or rotate the shoulder while the attacker maintains the chosen configuration.

**Defensive-grip recognition** (Replace an undirected pulling contest with a specific problem.)
Identify how the defender joins their hands and study the corresponding separation option without racing into extension.

**Orientation changes** (Understand why a configuration may require adjustment.)
Compare the same armbar control while the defender lies on their back and while they begin to turn.



</section>

<section id="implementation-sequence" class="content-section">

## Implementation Sequence
1. **Choose top or bottom**: Start from one familiar mount or guard entry. Record where control of the elbow and shoulder first becomes available.


2. **Stop at the armbar position**: End repetitions before any finishing pressure. Let the defender make a small, agreed attempt to retract the elbow so both partners can assess retention.


3. **Add a defensive grip**: Have the defender connect their hands in one agreed way. Study the matching separation lesson with a coach and reset before extension.


4. **Test a change of orientation**: Allow a slow turn. Notice whether the original control follows the shoulder or leaves room for the arm to escape.


5. **Compare the entry with the outcome**: Return to the starting mount or guard and repeat the full control sequence. Count retained positions separately from completed submissions.




</section>

<section id="common-obstacles" class="content-section hide-minimal">

## What Challenges Will You Face?
- **The elbow escapes during the transition.**: Shorten the entry and stop at the moment shoulder control disappears.
- **The attacker pulls against joined hands without changing the situation.**: Name the grip and return to a specific separation study task.
- **A turn is treated as a cue to extend faster.**: Remove finishing pressure and examine how the armbar position follows the turn.
- **Top and bottom armbar results are mixed together.**: Track the starting position so improvements can be attributed to the relevant entry.


</section>

<section id="assessment-metrics" class="content-section">

## How to Measure Your Progress
**Entry retention**: Observe whether the target arm remains controlled at the end of the transition.
Proficiency indicators:
- Names the entry
- Identifies elbow withdrawal
- Can stop in the control position


**Grip diagnosis**: Assess recognition of the defensive hand connection.
Proficiency indicators:
- Describes the grip
- Selects a relevant lesson
- Separates the drill from extension


**Orientation awareness**: Check what changes when the defender turns.
Proficiency indicators:
- Notices shoulder movement
- Identifies lost control
- Resets before forcing a finish


**Stage-specific review**: Classify the limiting problem after each short round.
Proficiency indicators:
- Distinguishes entry failure
- Distinguishes control failure
- Distinguishes grip-separation difficulty




</section>

<section id="training-methodology" class="content-section hide-minimal">

## How to Train This System Effectively

### Drilling Approach
BJJGraph suggests a stop-at-control drill: begin with a familiar mount entry, pause in the armbar position and let the defender make a small elbow-withdrawal attempt. In a separate round, add one defensive hand grip. Keep separation work distinct from finishing pressure so a coach can identify whether entry, retention or grip management needs attention.

### Progression Path
**Entry** (Focus: Reach the chosen armbar position without losing the targeted arm.)
**Retention** (Focus: Observe elbow withdrawal and shoulder-turn responses.)
**Separation** (Focus: Study one joined-hands problem with a clear reset.)
**Connection** (Focus: Combine the same entry and control task under modest resistance.)


### Common Mistakes
- Changing the entry before understanding why the elbow escapes.
- Using extension pressure to compensate for lost shoulder control.
- Measuring all armbar practice by taps alone.


</section>
